short: The Qing empire at its widest and richest, and the beginning of its exhaustion.
full:
Hongli took the throne on 18 October 1735 and ruled a Qing empire at its height. His Ten Great Campaigns carried the frontier deep into Central Asia; the destruction of the Dzungars in the 1750s brought Xinjiang under Qing control and came close to annihilating a people. He was a compulsive collector and cataloguer, and the Siku Quanshu, an imperial compilation of some 3,400 works, doubled as a literary inquisition in which thousands of texts were censored or destroyed.

He had pledged not to reign longer than his grandfather, the Kangxi Emperor, who held the throne for sixty-one years, and on 9 February 1796 he abdicated in favour of his son, the Jiaqing Emperor. The deference was formal only: as retired emperor he kept the seals, the audiences and the decisions until he died on 7 February 1799. By then campaigns and southern tours had drained the treasury, his favourite Heshen had accumulated a fortune said to rival the state's, the White Lotus rebellion was in its third year, and Macartney's embassy of 1793 had been dismissed with the remark that China had no use for British manufactures.
